signal.title: Make the scheduler idle-close deadline monotonic
signal.text: ## What changed? The idle-close deadline for CHASM (V2) schedules is now monotonic, and the Generator no longer re-arms an idle task it has already armed. **1. `SchedulerState.last_event_time` (new field 13)** — a persisted high water mark for the last "event" on the schedule (create, update, or action start). - `computeLastEventTime` — the previous `getLastEventTime` body, renamed, documented as non-monotonic. - `getLastEventTime` — read-only; floors the recomputed value at the persisted mark. - `advanceLastEventTime` — forward-only write, called from the Generator tick, which is the only place that arms an idle task. The mark is therefore durable before any `Validate` reads it back. **2. Skip redundant re-arms** — the Generator returns early when `IdleCloseTime` already equals the computed deadline, emitting `ScheduleIdleTask{outcome=skipped, reason=already_armed}`. Also updated the now-stale comment in `SchedulerIdleTaskHandler.Validate` that said a regression "shouldn't happen if getLastEventTime is monotonic". ## Why? `getLastEventTime` maxed over `Invoker.recentActions()`, which reads `BufferedStarts` — truncated by `applyCompletedRetention` to the last `recentActionCount` (10) completed entries, **ordered by `CloseTime`**. Whenever completion order differs from start order, evicting the start that held the largest `StartTime` drags the value, and therefore the idle deadline, backwards. Two distinct defects follow: 1. **The schedule closes earlier than its retention window allows.** `Validate` detects the regression, logs `"idle deadline regressed"`, and fires anyway. 2. **Unbounded growth of the mutable state blob and the timer queue.** Idle tasks are reaped only via `Validate`, whose predicate (`idleExpiration.After(scheduledTime)`) drops a task only when the deadline moved *later*. A flat or regressed deadline invalidates nothing, so every Generator tick leaves another task behind — one per action between idle ticks. Monotonicity alone fixes (1) but not (2): a same-instant action burst leaves the deadline *flat*, and the reap predicate doesn't fire on equality either. Hence the second change. ### Observed in production Two shapes, with very different profiles. **Duplicate arming is universal.** Over 30 days on one cell, comparing the two outcomes of the same counter: | | production namespaces (70) | all namespaces (97) | |---|---|---| | stray tasks reaped, `invalidated`/`closed` | 270,503 | 374,883 | | idle closes, `fired` | 268,716 | 373,104 | | ratio | **1.0** | **1.0** | Ratio across the 67 namespaces where both series are nonzero: min 0.79, p50 **1.00**, p90 **1.00**, max 1.50 — no namespace above 1.5. So essentially every schedule that closes via its idle timer carries exactly **two** idle tasks: one fires, one is stray. Trivial per schedule; ~270k stray task entries and an equal number of redundant physical timers per month on a single cell. That ratio is also the fleet-wide evidence for the monotonicity half of this PR. A ratio near *zero* would mean the second arm advanced the deadline and `Validate` reaped the first as `expiration_shift`. A ratio of 1.0 means the duplicate survived to close, i.e. **the deadline failed to advance on ~100% of idle closes.** **Heavy accumulation is a rarer tail**, requiring many action completions to arrive *after* the schedule has gone idle — in practice, a backfill. Sampling 951 V2 schedules across 13 namespaces in a second cell: 944 are structurally immune (perpetual recurring spec, or paused and held open by `isHeldOpen`), 7 are exposed, and 3 of those 7 carry 42–43 idle tasks. The worst walks its deadline monotonically *backwards* across 14 distinct values: ``` tc 12..24 -> ...06.649937Z (13 tasks) tc 25 -> ...06.618144Z tc 26 -> ...06.615669Z ... tc 48..52 -> ...06.463816Z tc 53 -> ...06.435762Z ``` 13 regressions, **214ms** of cumulative backwards drift, and **14 physical timers** — one per distinct deadline. It will close 214ms early, firing the tc-53 task rather than the tc-12 one. The other two drifted 1.5ms and 0.8ms with 2 timers each, so the drift is cumulative and proportional to how much the retention window churns, not a constant. For contrast, a healthy perpetual schedule with **643 transitions** carries **2 generate tasks at one distinct time and 0 idle tasks**. The generate task self-cleans because it has a high water mark (`validateTaskHighWaterMark`) that invalidates stale copies. The idle task is the only task in this component without one — which is what this PR adds. ## How did you test it? - [x] built - [x] covered by existing tests - [x] added new unit test(s) New file `chasm/lib/scheduler/scheduler_idle_deadline_test.go`, 10 tests. Verified they fail without the fix by reverting both production changes — 9 of 10 fail, reproducing the production numbers: ``` TestGeneratorTask_IdleTask_NotReArmedWhenDeadlineUnchanged expected: 1 actual: 21 # 20 no-op ticks -> 21 tasks, one per tick TestGeneratorTask_IdleTask_DoesNotAccumulateAcrossActionBurst idle deadline regressed at action 10: 2026-08-28 04:43:25.199231 -> 2026-08-28 04:43:25.197731 ``` A 1.5ms regression at action 10 — landing exactly where `recentActionCount = 10` first evicts. The tenth test (`NotArmedWhileSpecHasWork`) passes before and after by design; it guards against the skip logic swallowing the non-idle branch. Coverage: the root cause independent of the idle machinery (recomputed value regresses on eviction, floored read does not, mark never moves backwards, nil mark degrades to old behaviour); accumulation (repeated no-op ticks, and 43 actions completing one at a time through the retention window); stuck-open safety for the skip guard (deadline advance re-arms and reaps, pause/unpause re-arms, live spec arms nothing); `Validate` no longer entering the regressed branch after an eviction; and a sanity test that the snapshot helper sees armed tasks so the count assertions can't pass vacuously. Whole package green, stable under `-count=3 -test.shuffle=on`, `make lint-code` 0 issues, `go build ./...` and `go test ./chasm/...` clean. ## Potential risks **Rollout is inert both ways.** `last_event_time` is nil on every existing schedule, where `getLastEventTime` degrades to exactly the old recompute — nothing changes until the first Generator tick writes the mark. A downgrade ignores the field (proto3 Go keeps it in `unknownFields`, so a re-upgrade retains it) and reverts to today's behaviour. **Direction of change is safe.** Where the fix bites, the deadline holds instead of sliding earlier, so schedules close **later, never earlier**. The mark is a max over real events, so it cannot exceed the true last-event time — no unbounded extension of an entity's lifetime. **V1→V2 migration needs no change.** `LegacyToCreateFromMigrationStateRequest` leaves the field nil; `newSchedulerWithState`'s immediate `Generate()` seeds it from the migrated `BufferedStarts` before retention trims them. Two things for reviewers to weigh in on: - **`anchorLastEventTo` now rewrites `LastEventTime`, not just `Info`.** Three existing tests backdated `Info` to simulate an old last-event time, which the mark correctly resists. Production never lowers the mark (`Info.CreateTime` written once, `Info.UpdateTime` only moves forward), so this is a fixture constructing a hypothetical persisted state — but worth a second opinion that no real path can put `Info` behind the mark. - **The skip guard is best-effort.** It reads `IdleCloseTime` rather than the pending task list, because a component cannot introspect its own tasks. `IdleCloseTime` is cleared on the non-idle branch, so a schedule that goes non-idle and returns to idle at an *identical* deadline would arm a duplicate. I could not construct that path — every transition out of held-open bumps `Info.UpdateTime`, which advances the deadline — and two tests pin exactly one task through those transitions. Worst case is 2 duplicates rather than 43. ## Severity Two defects with different profiles, both addressed here: - **Duplicate arming: universal, small.** One stray task and one redundant physical timer per idle close, ~270k/month on one cell's production namespaces. Fixed by the skip guard. - **Deadline regression and heavy accumulation: rare, larger.** Needs an action burst arriving after the schedule goes idle. Fixed by the high water mark. Neither causes a misfire, and the early close is sub-second in every observed case, so this is a correctness-and-hygiene fix rather than an incident. Limits of the measurement: `reason="closed"` also fires when a correctly-armed single task is dropped because the schedule was deleted, terminated, or migrated to V1 — `Closed` has four setters. That inflates the stray-task count slightly; it is isolated enough to spot (one sampled namespace shows 1,353 `closed` with zero `fired`, i.e. entirely deletions). Only one cell was measured for the ratio, and the 951-schedule structural sample cannot see schedules exposed via `LimitedActions` with `RemainingActions == 0`, since `temporal schedule list` returns no `state` — so the "7 exposed" figure is a lower bound. ## Not in scope `Invoker.recordExecuteResult` stamps `StartTime` (raising the deadline) but calls only `addTasks()`, never `Generate()`, so an armed idle task can be invalidated as `expiration_shift` and deleted with nothing arming a replacement — leaving the schedule permanently open. This PR is neutral on it: the recomputed deadline rises either way, and the mark only floors. Repro and write-up are on `scheduler-orphaned-idle-task-repro`, to be filed separately. 🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

signal.title: DeleteWorkerDeploymentVersion fails permanently when a version summary outlives its version workflow
signal.text: ### What are you really trying to do? Keep the number of Worker Deployment Versions per deployment under `matching.maxVersionsInDeployment` by periodically deleting drained versions, so that new versions can always register. ### Describe the bug A Worker Deployment can end up listing a version in `DescribeWorkerDeployment`'s `versionSummaries` **after that version's own entity/workflow no longer exists**. Once in that state the entry is **permanently undeletable**: `DeleteWorkerDeploymentVersion` runs against a version workflow that isn't there and fails on every attempt, forever. The entry keeps counting toward `maxVersionsInDeployment`, and any automated cleanup that walks `versionSummaries` and deletes drained versions fails on it indefinitely. Observed on **server 1.30.3** (CLI 1.6.x), Postgres persistence, one namespace with 30d retention. The three views disagree with each other for the same build ID (names below are anonymized; `worker-a` is a deployment with 1 current + 21 drained versions, `1.42.0-a1b2` is the oldest drained one, created ~24 days earlier): ``` $ temporal worker deployment describe --name default/worker-a -o json -> versionSummaries contains build ID 1.42.0-a1b2, drainageStatus "drained" $ temporal worker deployment describe-version \ --deployment-name default/worker-a --build-id 1.42.0-a1b2 ERROR error describing worker deployment version: build ID '1.42.0-a1b2' not found in Worker Deployment 'default/worker-a' $ temporal workflow describe \ --workflow-id temporal-sys-worker-deployment-version:default/worker-a/1.42.0-a1b2 ERROR failed describing workflow: workflow not found for ID: ... ``` So the deployment workflow's version list and the version entities have diverged. Deleting it fails deterministically: ``` $ temporal worker deployment delete-version \ --deployment-name default/worker-a --build-id 1.42.0-a1b2 --identity <managerIdentity> ERROR error deleting worker deployment version: something went wrong, please retry (36634b00) ``` The retry hint is misleading — it is not transient. Every invocation over ~2 days failed identically. ### Root cause as far as we could trace it The generic frontend error hides the real failure. The frontend logs only the wrapper: ``` {"level":"error","msg":"deployment client unexpected error","error":"activity error", "operation":"DeleteWorkerDeploymentVersion","deployment":"default/worker-a", "args":["default","1.42.0-a1b2"], "logging-call-at":"service/worker/workerdeployment/client.go:1266"} ``` The actual cause appears only in the **system worker** logs: ``` {"level":"error","msg":"Activity error.", "Namespace":"default","TaskQueue":"temporal-sys-per-ns-tq", "WorkflowID":"temporal-sys-worker-deployment:default/worker-a", "ActivityType":"DeleteWorkerDeploymentVersion","Attempt":1, "Error":"workflow execution already completed"} ``` i.e. the deployment workflow's `DeleteWorkerDeploymentVersion` activity targets the version workflow, finds it already completed/absent, and surfaces that as a non-actionable internal error instead of treating the desired end state (version gone) as satisfied. ### Suspected trigger Not conclusively established, so treat this as a hypothesis: the version workflow closed when the version drained and was then removed by **namespace retention** (30d here), while the deployment workflow — which continues-as-new and carries its version list forward — kept the summary entry. The affected version was the oldest in the deployment, consistent with it being the first to cross the retention boundary. If that is the mechanism, any long-lived deployment should accumulate these as versions age past retention. ### Minimal repro We do not have a clean synthetic repro, which is why the mechanism above is a hypothesis. It appeared naturally on a deployment with steady rollout churn. If retention is the trigger, the shape would be: register a version, make it current, supersede it so it drains, then let the version workflow age past the namespace retention, and attempt `delete-version` on it. ### Expected behaviour Any one of these would resolve it: 1. **`DeleteWorkerDeploymentVersion` is idempotent** — if the version workflow is already absent, remove the summary entry and return success rather than an internal error. This seems like the natural fix: the caller's intent is already satisfied. 2. **The deployment workflow prunes summaries** whose version entity no longer exists (e.g. on continue-as-new, or when a delete discovers the entity is missing). 3. Failing either, a **supported way to remove such an entry**. The only lever we can see is terminating `temporal-sys-worker-deployment:default/<name>` so the list is rebuilt, which is not viable in production because that workflow holds live routing config (current/ramping version). Separately, and independent of the fix: **`something went wrong, please retry (<id>)` for a permanent, non-retryable condition is hard to diagnose.** Propagating the activity's cause (or at least a distinct error type) to the caller would have saved most of this investigation. ### Impact Low severity but permanent and self-accumulating: - The stale entry consumes one slot against `maxVersionsInDeployment` (200 in our config) and can never be reclaimed. - Automated below-cap cleanup fails on it on every run. Ours ran every 6h and exited non-zero each time until we special-cased it: on a failed delete we now probe `describe-version` and, only if it reports the version as absent, count it as already-gone instead of a failure. That works, but it is a workaround for a state the server arguably shouldn't expose. ### Related Cross-referencing #10737, which covers version GC not reclaiming eligible drained versions at the cap. This looks like a distinct, second-order problem in the same area: there the versions *aren't* reclaimed, here a version *cannot* be reclaimed because the summary outlived the entity. ### Environment - Temporal Server: 1.30.3 (Helm, Postgres persistence, ES/advanced visibility not in use) - Temporal CLI: 1.6.x - Worker Deployment Versioning with an external controller managing rollouts; workflows are pinned by default - Relevant config: `matching.maxVersionsInDeployment: 200`; namespace retention 30d; `worker.buildIdScavengerEnabled: true`
